catalog_quote: Tonalità. A formola isolata delle voci costituite da varie radici, che in realtà non sono che voci semplici o monosillabiche, l'accento cade sull'ultima, mentre nel contesto del discorso può questa stessa voce o sillaba, assumere lo stesso rilievo delle altre. Così diventa poco pratico l'impiego di segni speciali di tonalità, e noi procureremo di adoperarli il meno possibile. [de Gregorio 1901: 145] ... 9. Der Wortton liegt meist auf der Endsilbe. 10. Gleichlautende Wörter werden mitunter durch die Intonation unterschieden. Wir unterscheiden dabei den steigenden und den fallenden Ton eines Vokals (ersterer durch á, letzterer durch à bezeichnet). [Seidel 1904: 40] ... Bei mehrsilbigen Wörtern hat die letzte Silbe in der Regel den Wortton. Die Satzbetonung ist, bis zum wichtigsten Worte in einer Steigerung begriffen, von da an fällt sie in einer Art von Cadenz. ... Man hat drei Tonstufen …
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Tonalità. A formola isolata delle voci costituite da varie radici, che in realtà non sono che voci semplici o monosillabiche, l'accento cade sull'ultima, mentre nel contesto del discorso può questa stessa voce o sillaba, assumere lo stesso rilievo delle altre. Così diventa poco pratico l'impiego di segni speciali di tonalità, e noi procureremo di adoperarli il meno possibile. [Concordant: Henrici 1891: 18 'Bei mehrsilbigen Wörtern hat die letzte Silbe in der Regel den Wortton.']
new_statements.translation: Tonality. In the isolated form of words made up of several roots -- which in reality are nothing but simple or monosyllabic words -- the accent falls on the last [syllable], whereas in connected discourse this same word or syllable may take on the same prominence as the others. Thus the use of special tonality marks becomes impractical, and we shall try to use them as little as possible. [Henrici 1891: 'In polysyllabic words the last syllable as a rule carries the word accent.']
new_statements.citation: de Gregorio, Giacomo. 1901. Sulla struttura della lingua evé (ewe, ephe, epe) in base a proprie raccolte dal vivo: osservazioni glottologiche. Studi glottologici italiani 2: 129-223.
new_statements.locator: p. 145, B) Fonetica, § 6, paragraph 'Tonalità' (PDF p. 158 of the archive.org scan studiglottologi01greggoog); informant identity p. 132, variety p. 142
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE CHECK., PDF p. 158 = printed p. 145 (running head 'LINGUA EVÉ. 145'), rendered and read: paragraph 'Tonalità. A formola isolata delle voci costituite da varie radici, che in realtà non sono che voci semplici o monosillabiche, l'accento cade sull'ultima, mentre nel contesto del discorso può questa stessa voce o sillaba, assumere lo stesso rilievo delle altre. Così diventa poco pratico l'impiego di segni speciali di tonalità, e noi procureremo di adoperarli il meno possibile.' -- verbatim as reported (also scanned lines 6954-6959 of). It follows a 'Quantità' paragraph and precedes sec. 7 consonants, i.e. it is the whole of what de Gregorio says on prosody. Concordant Henrici 1891 p. 18…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In citation (isolated) forms of polysyllabic words, prominence ('accento'/'Wortton') is heard on the final syllable; in connected speech this final prominence is levelled. Both 1891/1901 observers otherwise recognise lexically distinctive pitch (Henrici: Hochton/Tiefton/Tonlosigkeit). Modern descriptions analyse Gen as a two-toneme (H/L) language (Bolé-Richard 1983: 118; Gblem-Poidi 2017: 15; Lotven 2020: H, L, marginal HL) and, as far as could be seen, say nothing about word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: de Gregorio: in connected discourse the final syllable may have no more relief than the others. Henrici 1891: 104 notes demonstratives (ehe, esi, eke...) with 'Ton' on the first syllable; 'in der Regel' (as a rule) hedges the final-syllable rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms only; explicitly neutralised at phrase level per de Gregorio. Both statements are pre-tonological impressionistic observations (1891, 1901) that do not separate stress from lexical tone; Gen is a tone language and the modern primary description (Bolé-Richard 1983, seen only in snippets) lists tone as the sole oppositional prosodic feature of the syllable with no accent feature. Treat 'fixed-final' as the historical observers' percept, not an established modern analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: de Gregorio 1901 is based on a native of Klein-Popo/Anecho (Aného) and states that Anecho is the variety principally studied (pp. 132, 142) = Gen genn1243 (Capo's Anexo dialect). Henrici 1891 covers 'Ephe' across three dialects -- Anlo (= Ewe, ewee1241), Anecho (= Gen, genn1243) and Dahome (= Fon, fonn1241) -- so his p. 18 rule is not Gen-specific. Lotven 2020 describes a speaker from Batonou, Togo (Gengbe). Westermann 1907 is Ewe proper (ewee1241), context only.

sources.locator: p. 145, B) Fonetica, § 6, paragraph 'Tonalità' (PDF p. 158 of the archive.org scan studiglottologi01greggoog); informant identity p. 132, variety p. 142
sources.note: p. 145 'Tonalità': in isolation forms of (poly-radical) words the accent falls on the last syllable; in connected discourse that syllable may have no more relief than the others, so he uses tone/accent marks sparingly. Informant native of Klein-Popo/Anecho (p. 132); 'l'Anecho... la varietà da noi principalmente studiata' (p. 142). Pre-tonological, impressionistic.

sources.citation: Henrici, Ernst. 1891. Lehrbuch der Ephe-Sprache (Ewe): Anlo-, Anecho- und Dahome-Mundart, mit Glossar und einer Karte der Sklavenküste. Stuttgart & Berlin: W. Spemann.
sources.note: p. 18 'Wort- und Satzbetonung, Intonation': 'Bei mehrsilbigen Wörtern hat die letzte Silbe in der Regel den Wortton.' Then distinguishes three musical 'Tonstufen' (Hochton, Tiefton, Tonlosigkeit) that are lexically distinctive. Scope is 'Ephe' across Anlo (Ewe), Anecho (Gen) and Dahome (Fon) dialects; p. 104 demonstratives 'Der Ton liegt bei allen auf der ersten Silbe'.

sources.citation: Westermann, Diedrich. 1907. Grammatik der Ewe-Sprache. Berlin: Dietrich Reimer.
sources.note: Context only (Ewe proper, ewee1241, Anlo-based): sec. 58 p. 38 'Starkton' -- the first high tone of a sentence/compound sounds somewhat stronger, purely physiological; Ewe 'kennt keine Betonung' governed by content; only the fixed syllable tones matter. Not a Gen description.

sources.citation: Lotven, Samson. 2020. Sound system sketch of a Gengbe speaker from Batonou. IULC Working Papers 20(1), 27 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on word stress. Sec. 6 'Tone' (pp. 16-21): three lexically contrastive tones L, H, HL (HL only in loans/interjections/ideophones), derived LH; consonant-tone interaction. Only mention of stress: French loans 'where final stress is common' are borrowed with final falling tone (p. 20).
